question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+3 \cdot y=\left(x-2\right) \cdot y^{3}.
$$

Work on an interval where $\left(x-2\right)>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=3\\ q(x)&=\left(x-2\right)\\ n&=3.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{3}$ and set $z=y^{-2}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{2}{y^{3}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(-6\right)z=- 2 \cdot \left(x-2\right).$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int -6\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x-2\right)}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x-2\right)}\,z\right)=- 2 \cdot \left(x-2\right) \cdot e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x-2\right)}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x-2\right)}z=\frac{\left(\left(x-2\right) + \frac{1}{6}\right) \cdot e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x-2\right)}}{3}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{6 \cdot \left(x-2\right)} + \frac{\left(x-2\right)}{3} + \frac{1}{18}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-2}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\pm\sqrt{\frac{18}{18 \cdot C \cdot e^{6 \cdot \left(x-2\right)} + 6 \cdot \left(x-2\right) + 1}}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals. Both signs are retained wherever the radicand is positive.
